analysisMarkdown:
## Where the price sits

Gold spot is **$3,573.04**, up **0.85%** on the day — a modest bounce within a steep, well-established downtrend. Context matters more than the daily tick: spot is **35.0% below** its 52-week high of **$5,496** set on 2026-01-29, and only just above its 52-week low of **$3,533** printed on 2026-11-21. This is decidedly *not* record territory; it is the lower end of a punishing year.

The moving-average picture is firmly bearish. Spot trades **10.2% below** its 50-day average of **$3,978** and **15.3% below** its 200-day average of **$4,217**. Trailing returns are negative across every window that matters: **-12.0%** over 20 days, **-22.6%** over 90 days, and **-13.4%** over the past year. Annualised 20-day volatility of **30%** underlines how sharp the recent move has been, with the 20-day closing range spanning **$3,533 to $4,121**.

## The macro backdrop

Two forces weigh directly on gold. First, the **broad dollar index** sits at **123.60**, up **2.26** over 30 days and **5.54** over 90 days — higher than **100%** of readings in the past year. A dollar at a one-year high makes gold more expensive outside the US and is a classic headwind. Second, the **10-year real yield** is **2.79%**, up **0.13 pp** over 30 days and **0.47 pp** over 90 days, and higher than **92%** of the past year's readings. Elevated real yields raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset. The 10-year Treasury yield is **4.92%**, while the 10-year inflation breakeven has eased to **2.13%** — so the real-yield climb is being driven by rates, not fading inflation expectations.

## The events driving the market

The dominant theme is monetary policy. Hawkish Fed signals have reinforced market bets on a **December rate increase**, pushing the dollar and yields higher and pressuring gold. That repricing is the clearest, most recent catalyst behind the slide to a one-year low. Reinforcing the mood, a major bank trimmed its gold forecast earlier in the month, explicitly citing the Fed's more hawkish turn.

Looking ahead, markets are focused on **upcoming US inflation data**, which could shape the December decision. Because that release has not yet happened, it introduces two-way risk but does not justify shifting today's call. A softer print could ease the rate-hike narrative; a firm one would deepen the existing pressure.

Structural demand — notably continued central-bank buying — remains a feature of the market, but it is a standing condition rather than a dated event, and it has not arrested the downtrend. It is noted here for context, not as a reason to adjust the signal.

## Short-term outlook (1–4 weeks)

The short-term scorecard is deeply negative at **-5**, producing a baseline **SELL**. The components: a 20-day return of **-11.98%** (strongly adverse), price **10.18%** below the 50-day average (adverse), a rising real yield (adverse), and a dollar up **1.86%** over 30 days (strongly adverse). The only positive is a contrarian stretch reading — price has fallen far enough below its 50-day average to count as mildly supportive — but it is one green tile against four red.

No bullish dated event qualifies for an adjustment, so the call stands at **SELL, medium confidence**. The daily bounce does not change the setup. This view would be challenged by **a daily close above $4,121**.

## Long-term outlook (3–12 months)

The long-term scorecard is uniformly adverse at **-6**: price below both major averages, a bearish 50-day/200-day crossover, a 90-day return of **-22.58%**, a **34.98%** distance from the 52-week high, and both the real yield and dollar higher over 90 days. Every factor points the same way, and a hawkish Fed plus trimmed analyst forecasts keep the medium-term backdrop challenging.

The baseline is **SELL, high confidence**, with no qualifying event to adjust it. This view would be challenged by **a daily close above $4,673**.

## Risks to these views

The main risk to both bearish readings is a dovish surprise. A softer inflation print, a shift in Fed tone, or a sharp dollar reversal could relieve the two pressures — real yields and the dollar — that are doing most of the damage. Geopolitical shocks or a renewed surge in official-sector demand could also lift gold quickly, given how far and fast it has fallen. On the other side, the risks skew the same direction as the trend: a confirmed December hike or a further dollar advance would reinforce the SELL setups. As always, these signals describe market **conditions** over their horizons — they are not advice about any individual's holdings, timing, or risk tolerance.
